verses.note: The Spirit's first appearance in Scripture is at creation, present and active over what is not yet ordered. The Old Testament later speaks of the Spirit giving life (Psalm 104:30), a thread the New Testament picks up when it speaks of the Spirit's work of new creation.

The breath God gave in 2:7 is his to give and to withdraw. Human life depends moment by moment on God's Spirit (Psalm 104:29-30, Job 34:14-15), and this verse is the first time God says he will limit it.

In the Old Testament the Spirit of God gives wisdom, skill, and capacity to lead, not only prophecy. Pharaoh likely meant something within his own religion, but the narrator lets his words point to the true source of Joseph's gifts, as Nebuchadnezzar's words about Daniel will later do (Daniel 4:8).

The Messiah is the Spirit-bearer. The Gospels show the Spirit descending and remaining on Jesus at his baptism (John 1:32-33), and in Nazareth Jesus reads the related promise of Isaiah 61:1 as fulfilled in himself. Christian theology has drawn from this verse that the Son's human life was lived in dependence on the Spirit.

Jeremiah does not name the Spirit, but Ezekiel's parallel promise joins the new heart to God's Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:26-27), and Paul reads the two together when he calls the Corinthians a letter written ‘with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts’ (2 Corinthians 3:3).

The Old Testament knew the Spirit coming on judges, prophets, and kings for particular tasks. Here the Spirit is promised to the whole people, permanently, within, and for ordinary obedience. That promise is what Joel 2:28-29 announces and what Peter declares fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-18, 33).

The Spirit who will give life to the bones in verse 14 is first the Spirit who brings the prophet into the valley. The chapter begins and ends with God's Spirit acting: carrying the messenger, then raising the dead.

The Spirit is here the giver of life, the role the Nicene Creed confesses when it names the Holy Spirit as Lord and giver of life. Ezekiel ties the Spirit to both the new heart (36:26-27) and the raising of the dead, the two works Paul joins when he says the Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to believers' mortal bodies (Romans 8:11).

The grief that leads to cleansing (13:1) does not begin with the people; it begins when God pours out his Spirit. Repentance is presented as God's gift before it is the people's act, the pattern of Acts 2, where Peter's hearers are cut to the heart after the Spirit is poured out.

The prophets promised that God would pour out his Spirit on his people (Joel 2:28-29, Ezekiel 36:25-27). John says the coming one will do this, which assigns to Jesus a work the Old Testament reserves for God.
The Spirit comes upon Jesus to equip him as the anointed one, in line with Isaiah 42:1 and 61:1. The one who will baptize with the Spirit first receives the Spirit.

The Spirit who came on Jesus at his baptism (1:10) is the power at work in his exorcisms. To call that power unclean is to reject God's own presence in Jesus, which is why the sin is named as against the Spirit.
The Spirit who came upon Jesus at his baptism (1:10) will speak through his followers on trial. Acts shows it happening with Peter before the council (Acts 4:8).

John is filled with the Spirit before he can do anything, as Jeremiah was set apart before birth (Jeremiah 1:5). Luke contrasts two kinds of filling, wine and the Spirit, a contrast Paul makes too (Ephesians 5:18) and Pentecost dramatizes (Acts 2:13-17).
The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) comes upon Mary, and the life that results is holy from its beginning.
The Spirit fills Elizabeth and she speaks prophetically, the first of several in Luke's birth stories to do so (1:67, 2:25-27). The Spirit's first work in the Gospel is to recognize Jesus.
The Spirit who silenced nothing but doubt now opens Zechariah's mouth in prophecy. In Luke the Spirit's filling repeatedly issues in inspired speech (1:41-42, Acts 2:4, 4:31).
Three times in three verses the Spirit rests on, reveals to, and leads Simeon. Before Pentecost the Spirit is already at work among faithful Israelites waiting for God's promise.
The Messiah's work is to give the Spirit, something no prophet could do. The promise is fulfilled when the risen Jesus pours out the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 1:5, 2:33).

The Spirit does not remove Jesus from testing but leads him into it and through it. Luke's Christology is Spirit-shaped from the start: conceived by the Spirit (1:35), anointed at the Jordan (3:22), led in the wilderness (4:1), empowered in Galilee (4:14), and claiming Isaiah's anointing (4:18).
Luke places the Spirit's power at the beginning of Jesus' public work, as he will at the beginning of the church's (Acts 1:8, 2:4). The ministry that follows is the Spirit's work through the Son.

The witnesses are not sent in their own strength. The Spirit is the Father's promise, sent by the risen Son, and given as power for witness; the Trinitarian shape of the church's mission is already present in the Gospel's last words.

The Spirit rests on Jesus so that Jesus can give the Spirit to others. The Gospel keeps that promise when the risen Jesus breathes on the disciples and says ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (20:22); Acts 2 tells of the outpouring at Pentecost.
The Spirit is the agent of the new birth. Whatever the water means, the whole sentence makes the Spirit the one who gives entrance to the kingdom.

The Spirit is free. He cannot be commanded, predicted, or institutionally controlled, and yet his work is real and audible. The verse guards against making new birth either a human technique or an invisible idea without effects.

The Spirit rests on Jesus without limit, fulfilling the Baptist's sign that the Spirit would remain on him (1:32-33). Because the Spirit is his without measure, he can give the Spirit to others (7:39, 20:22).

John later identifies the living water as the Spirit, whom believers would receive after Jesus was glorified (7:37-39). Here the gift is offered on the sole condition of asking, which makes the Spirit a gift of grace, not a reward for purity or pedigree.

The water Jesus gives does not stay outside the believer. It becomes a spring within, a source that keeps rising. John's picture of the Spirit is of God's own life taking up residence in a person and continuing to give life from inside.

‘In spirit’ refers first to the Holy Spirit whom Jesus gives (verses 10 and 14, 7:39), not to human sincerity. The Spirit makes worship possible in any place, because the Spirit unites worshipers to the Son, who is the truth (14:6).

Life comes through the Spirit, and the Spirit comes through Jesus' words. Whatever else the discourse means, it cannot mean that life comes by a physical process apart from the Spirit and faith; on this every Christian tradition agrees, while differing on what the Spirit uses.

On either punctuation the water is the Spirit (7:39), and its source is Jesus. If the believer is the channel, the Spirit received from Christ overflows through the believer to others; if Christ is the fountain, the verse fixes the eye on him. The two readings differ in emphasis, not in substance.

The Spirit's coming depends on Jesus' glorification. The gift is not a separate blessing apart from the cross but its fruit, which is why Jesus breathes the Spirit on the disciples only after his resurrection (20:22) and why Peter at Pentecost ties the outpouring to the exalted Christ (Acts 2:33).

Wind and fire are Old Testament signs of God's presence (Exodus 3:2, 19:18; Ezekiel 37:9). Their coming on each person, not on the group as a whole or on the apostles alone, says that the Spirit now rests on every member of the community, as he rested on Jesus at his baptism.
The Spirit is the giver of the speech. The disciples do not produce the gift and then ascribe it to God; Luke says the Spirit kept giving them the words.

In the Old Testament the Spirit came on particular people: prophets, judges, kings, craftsmen. Joel promised a day when the Spirit would come on all God's people without distinction of sex, age, or status, and Peter says that day has come.
The Spirit's coming is the exalted Christ's gift. The Spirit does not replace Jesus but comes from him and testifies to his reign.

The Holy Spirit is God's gift to every believer, and his work here is to make God's love known in the heart. The Spirit does not add a second love to God's love in Christ; he pours that love in, so that it is known by experience as well as by report.

The ‘new way of the Spirit’ is the first mention of the Spirit since 5:5, and it announces the theme of chapter 8. The contrast between letter and Spirit echoes 2:29 and 2 Corinthians 3:6, and behind them the promise of a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33, Ezekiel 36:27).
The Spirit is ‘the Spirit of life’, the giver of life promised in Ezekiel 37:14, and the power that sets believers free. Freedom from sin's rule is the Spirit's work in those joined to Christ.
The Spirit shapes not only conduct but the direction of the mind. Paul describes two whole ways of being human, and the Spirit's way is ‘life and peace’, echoing the peace with God of 5:1.

The verse makes the Spirit's indwelling the mark of every believer, not of a spiritual elite. That has been important in debates over whether receiving the Spirit is a second experience after conversion: Pentecostal and holiness traditions distinguish a later baptism in the Spirit for power, while other traditions hold that every believer receives the Spirit at conversion.
Being led by the Spirit marks God's children. The verse ties the Spirit's leading to the moral struggle of verse 13, not to private revelation.

The Spirit's witness is the ground of Christian assurance. John Wesley preached two sermons titled The Witness of the Spirit on verse 16, teaching that the Spirit gives a direct inner testimony that a believer is God's child, confirmed by the fruit of the Spirit. Reformed writers such as the Westminster Confession (18.2) locate assurance in God's promises, the evidence of grace, and the Spirit's witness together.

The Spirit is a person who helps, intercedes, and groans, not an impersonal force. His intercession within believers (here) and Christ's at the Father's right hand (verse 34) form a double intercession.
The Spirit who now lives in believers (6:19) will fully give life to their bodies at the resurrection (Romans 8:11). The resurrection body is the Spirit's work completed.

The risen Christ ‘became a life-giving spirit’: not that he became a spirit without a body, but that in his resurrection he is so joined to the Spirit's work that he gives the Spirit's life to his people (compare 2 Corinthians 3:17-18).

The Spirit is the mark of belonging to God's people. Paul assumes the Galatians knew when they received the Spirit, and he makes that experience the evidence that they were already fully accepted before any law was imposed on them.

The blessing promised to Abraham finds its content in the gift of the Spirit. The Spirit promised by the prophets for the last days comes to Gentiles as well as Jews, through faith, as the fruit of Christ's death.

The Spirit is both seal (God's mark of ownership and protection) and down payment (the first installment of the life to come). His presence now guarantees the inheritance later. Circumcision had been called a seal (Romans 4:11), and second-century writers such as the Shepherd of Hermas (Similitudes 9.16) spoke of baptism as ‘the seal’; here the seal is the Spirit himself.
The Spirit who sealed believers (verse 13) also gives wisdom and revelation. Knowing God is not only a matter of study but of the Spirit's illumination, which Paul asks for on behalf of others.
God's dwelling among his people is by the Spirit. The chapter ends Trinitarian, as verse 18 did: in the Lord Jesus, a dwelling for God, by the Spirit.
The Spirit is the speaker of Scripture, addressing each generation with the same ‘today’. His voice is heard in the reading of the text.

The descriptions include sharing in the Holy Spirit, the gift poured out in the community's life (2:4). Whatever else the verse means, it places the people it describes inside the church's experience of the Spirit, not outside it.

Universal knowledge of God is what the prophets associated with the outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, young and old, servant and free (Joel 2:28-29). In the new covenant access to God is not restricted to priests or prophets.

The Holy Spirit not only inspired Scripture but also taught through the structures God commanded. The verse gives the Spirit the role of disclosing what the old order meant, which is how Hebrews reads the Old Testament throughout.

The Holy Spirit is presented as the one who speaks in Scripture and bears witness now. Hebrews ties the Spirit's testimony to the new covenant, whose promise of an inward law the Spirit fulfills (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

The Holy Spirit is called ‘the Spirit of grace’, a phrase that echoes Zechariah 12:10, where God pours out a spirit of grace and supplication. To reject Christ is not only to spurn a doctrine but to insult the gracious Spirit who brought the gospel home.
